deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a verbatim English excerpt, with ellipses, from David Brewster's biography of Newton (The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, London 1831, ch. on the Principia, around pp. 154-157). It continues directly from the previous page (folio 38r, headed in German 'Geschichte der in den Principien veröffentlichten Entdeckungen Newtons').

The excerpt narrates the publication history of the Principia:
(i) Halley and Paget were asked to remind Newton of his promise to register De Motu 'for securing the invention to himself'.
(ii) On 25 Feb 1684/5 Secretary Aston read Newton's letter agreeing to enter his 'notions about motion' in the register.
(iii) Newton's work was interrupted by a five- or six-week visit to Lincolnshire.
(iv) The manuscript, titled Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica and dedicated to the Society, was presented by Dr. Vincent on 28 April 1686, with Sir John Hoskins (Hooke's friend) in the chair. The copyist's marginal note is 'ec. (Streit mit Hooke)', i.e. 'etc. (dispute with Hooke)', marking an omitted passage.
(v) Printing was referred to the Council; on 19 May it was resolved to print at the Society's expense, with Halley superintending. Halley's letter of 22 May reported this.
(vi) Newton's reply of 20 June 1686 threatens to suppress Book III ('Philosophy is such an impertinently litigious lady...'). It also mentions his provisional retitling as 'De Motu Corporum Libri duo' before keeping the original title.
(vii) Halley's reply of 29 June begs him not to suppress Book III, the part 'acceptable to those who will call themselves philosophers without mathematics'.
(viii) Book II was presented on 2 March 1686/7 and Book III on 6 April 1687; the work was 'completed in May 1687'.

The deleted words show copying slips by eye-skip:
- 'The third book' was struck out and the copyist resumed at 'I designed the whole...'.
- 'as much the greater number' was struck out because the copyist jumped ahead to the end of Halley's sentence.

There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically. The page serves as historical background, probably for Riemann's interest in the foundations of Newtonian gravitation and action at a distance in his Naturphilosophie notes. The English hand may not be Riemann's own, and the excerpt may have been copied by or for him.
errors: No mathematical content, hence no mathematical errors.

Historical detail inherited from Brewster: the Principia was actually published around 5 July 1687 (Halley's letter to Newton of that date), not merely 'completed in May 1687'. Pepys's imprimatur is dated 5 July 1686.

Brewster places the Council resolution on 19 May. The Society's meeting of 19 May 1686 ordered printing, but the Council's decision that Halley would undertake the business at his own charge came on 2 June 1686. The copied account smooths this over.
Copying slips in the manuscript: the eye-skip deletions 'The third book' and 'as much the greater number'; 'no' and 'but she gives' added interlinearly to repair omissions in the Newton quotation.

results.what: Historical excerpt on the genesis and publication of Newton's Principia (Halley correspondence, Hooke priority dispute)
results.modern_name: History of the publication of the Principia (1686-87)
results.usually_credited_to: David Brewster, Life of Sir Isaac Newton (1831), drawing on Royal Society records and Newton-Halley letters

deep.surprise_reason: This is a reading excerpt copied from Brewster's well-known Newton biography, with no original mathematical or scientific content. Riemann's interest in Newton's gravitation and action at a distance is already known from his Naturphilosophie fragments.
transcription_corrections: Line 'the MS. should be printed': the image appears to read 'MSS.' (Brewster has 'MS.').
'The third I now design[?] to suppress': the image shows 'design' with a corrected or struck final letter. Brewster's text reads 'design to suppress', so the '[?]' can be removed.
'on the 29th June': the image reads '29the June' (a slip for 29th).
'as I guess by what you write': the image shows a closing quotation mark placed before 'as I guess', a copying artifact of the eye-skip deletion.
The interlinear additions 'no' (in 'can no sooner') and 'but she gives' are correctly marked as insertions.
